solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: I'll enter to fasten Nancy's black gown

indicators.note: the clue says the I will go into the word for fasten, so one piece sits inside another

parts.note: to peg something is to fasten it, as with a clothes peg
I will: the letter I is the one that does the entering
Nancy is a city in France, and the French word for black is noir

explanation.surface: Someone announces they will step in to do up a Frenchwoman's dark dressing gown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nancy' looks like a woman's name but is the French city, which tells you to use a French word.
explanation.definitionFit: A peignoir is a woman's light loose dressing gown, so the plain word for robe fits.

clue.text: Stress when one supports English speed limits in Shropshire

indicators.note: in a down clue a piece that supports another sits below it, so the I comes after the AS

parts.note: MPH, miles per hour, is a measure of speed
as can mean when, as in 'as he left'
I is the Roman numeral for one

indicators.note: the limits of a word are its first and last letters, here of Shropshire

explanation.surface: A traffic report notes where English speed limits are enforced in Shropshire, a rural county in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supports' puts the I beneath AS in this down entry; 'limits in' takes the outside letters of Shropshire, S and E.
explanation.definitionFit: To stress a point and to underline its importance are synonyms, both verbs.

clue.text: Boss retains area with a fruit tree

indicators.note: the boss word holds the area letter within it

parts.note: guv, short for governor, is informal British for the boss

explanation.surface: A manager keeps a patch of ground that has a fruit tree on it.
explanation.definitionFit: The guava is a tropical tree grown for its fruit, so it is an example of a fruit tree.

clue.text: Excessively big deliveries mailman's core rage, possibly

parts.note: in cricket an over is a set of six deliveries from the bowler

indicators.note: the core of a word is its central letter, here the middle of mailman
possibly says the letters of rage might be arranged in another way

explanation.surface: A postman fumes over far too many parcels to deliver.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deliveries' looks like the postman's parcels but is a cricket over. The middle letter of mailman is L, and 'possibly' turns RAGE into ARGE.
explanation.definitionFit: Overlarge means too great in size, a plain synonym for excessively big.

clue.text: Gentleman returned fish dish

indicators.note: returned says the title is read back to front

parts.note: sir is the respectful title for a gentleman
the sole is a flatfish

explanation.surface: A gentleman sends back his fish course at a restaurant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returned' turns SIR into RIS. 'fish dish' reads as one phrase, but only 'dish' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A rissole is a fried cake of minced meat or fish, so it is an example of a dish.

clue.text: Billion netted by old firm

indicators.note: a thing netted by another is caught inside it

parts.note: stale means old and no longer fresh

explanation.surface: A billion is earned by a long-established company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'firm' looks like a noun for a company, but it is the adjective meaning steady.
explanation.definitionFit: Stable and firm are synonyms describing something steady and not likely to move.

clue.text: One's pointed to lace

definitions.meaning: something with a sharp point, like a nail or a tall thin piece of metal
to secretly add alcohol or a drug to someone's drink

explanation.surface: A shoemaker explains which tool is used for threading laces.
explanation.definitionFit: A spike is a pointed object, and spiking a drink means lacing it, a verb sense.

clue.text: I'll mess about after a year without purpose

indicators.note: the jumbled letters come after the a
about means the letters of I'll mess are moved around

explanation.surface: Someone promises to drift around for a year with no aim.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'around' in the surface, but it signals the anagram of the letters in I'll mess.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something aimlessly means doing it with no goal, so it matches without purpose.

clue.text: Failure is more imminent without leader

indicators.note: without its leader means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: something more imminent is nearer in time, closer

explanation.surface: A collapse is getting nearer with nobody in charge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without leader' drops the C from CLOSER.
explanation.definitionFit: A failure is a person who never succeeds, the same as someone called a no-hoper.

clue.text: Daughter's accepted by university — spread the latest news!

indicators.note: the daughter letter is taken in by the following letters

parts.note: pâté is a paste spread on toast
D is the usual abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A proud parent wants everyone to hear that their daughter got into university.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spread' looks like a verb telling you to tell everyone, but it is pâté, the paste.
explanation.definitionFit: An update is a report giving recent information, so it suits the latest news.

clue.text: Brush him off? Risk's involved with that

indicators.note: involved means mixed up, so the jumbled him and risk's are tangled together into one word
off, as in gone off or out of order, says the letters of him are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone advises giving a man the brush-off, as dealing with him is risky.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brush' and 'off' look like the phrasal verb, but 'Brush' alone is the definition and 'off' signals the anagram; 'involved with that' just ties the clue together.
explanation.definitionFit: A brush is a short minor fight, the same sense as a small clash between forces.

clue.text: Capture wild animal in South Africa close to cape? That's sweet

parts.note: ZA is the international code for South Africa
to bag something is to catch it
the lion is a wild animal

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter, here of cape

explanation.surface: A hunter bags a lion near the Cape in South Africa and celebrates.
explanation.walkthrough: 'close to' takes E, the last letter of cape.
explanation.definitionFit: Zabaglione is an Italian dessert of whipped egg yolks, sugar and wine, so it is a pudding.

clue.text: Portion of apple crumble is greyish-brown

indicators.note: Portion of says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A slice of apple crumble has a dull brownish colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is the pale beige colour of unbleached linen, a light greyish-brown shade.

clue.text: Spot the female music-maker

parts.note: a zit is a pimple or spot on the skin
her is the pronoun for a female

explanation.surface: Someone picks out the woman playing an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spot' looks like a verb meaning notice, but it is the noun for a pimple.
explanation.definitionFit: A zither is a stringed instrument, an example of something that produces music.

clue.text: Henry Cooper so confounded predictions

parts.note: H is the symbol for the henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: confounded means mixed up, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Henry Cooper, a British boxing champion, baffled the pundits with his results.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confounded' rearranges COOPERSO into OROSCOPE.
explanation.definitionFit: A horoscope is a forecast from the positions of the stars, so it gives predictions.

clue.text: Discharge duty with energy

parts.note: E is the symbol for energy in physics
a mission is a task or duty one is sent on

explanation.surface: Someone carries out their job with plenty of vigour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discharge duty' reads as one phrase, but 'Discharge' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An emission is something sent out or released, the same sense as a discharge of gas.

clue.text: Wife interrupts popular performer's ball

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: the wife letter breaks into the letters that follow

parts.note: a singer is a performer

explanation.surface: A wife cuts in on a well-known performer at a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ball' looks like a dance, but it is a cricket delivery. An inswinger is a ball that swerves in towards the batter.
explanation.definitionFit: In cricket an inswinger is a delivery that curves in the air towards the batter, an example of a bowled delivery.

clue.text: Worker has to choose clothing a long time before I have

indicators.note: the first part comes before the remaining letters
clothing means wrapping around, so the long time goes inside

parts.note: to opt is to choose
an era is a long period of time
I've is the contraction of I have

explanation.surface: A worker has to pick an outfit, which takes far longer than I do.
explanation.definitionFit: An operative is a factory or machine worker, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Prince periodically is entertained by King's students

indicators.note: to be entertained by is to be taken in as a guest, so it goes inside

parts.note: King Lear is Shakespeare's tragic king, with the possessive 's

indicators.note: periodically means taking every other letter, here the second, fourth and sixth of Prince

explanation.surface: A prince is sometimes a guest at a monarch's college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'periodically' takes the even letters of Prince. The king is Shakespeare's King Lear.
explanation.definitionFit: Learners are people being taught, so the word is a synonym for students.

clue.text: Nick hastily got together cash, having no handicap

definitions.meaning: a nick is a small cut or graze
a team assembled in a hurry from whoever is available is a ... side
a golfer with zero handicap is a ... player

explanation.surface: Someone quickly scraped together money, with no head start to help.
explanation.definitionFit: Scratch means a small cut, a hurriedly assembled side, slang for money, and a golfer playing off zero.

clue.text: Designated journalist is next to pen line

indicators.note: the journalist's letters are placed next to the others

parts.note: a sty is a pen for pigs
ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A named reporter sits beside the person writing the next line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' looks like a writing tool, but it is a farm enclosure.
explanation.definitionFit: To be styled is to be called or named by a title, so it means designated.

clue.text: Cockney listens — using these

indicators.note: a Cockney, a working-class Londoner, traditionally drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: someone who listens hears

explanation.surface: A Londoner listens with the organs made for the purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is from London's East End; 'Cockney' drops the H from HEARS. The whole clue also defines: you listen using your ears.
explanation.definitionFit: We hear with these organs, so the whole clue describes what a Londoner listens with.

clue.text: In Greece, a river with origin in Athens

parts.note: Alph is the sacred river in Coleridge's poem Kubla Khan

indicators.note: the origin of a word is its first letter, here of Athens

explanation.surface: A traveller in Greece sees a river that rises in Athens.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In Greece, a' looks like scene-setting, but it is the definition: the Greek letter for a.
explanation.definitionFit: Alpha is the first letter of the Greek alphabet, the Greek equivalent of our letter a.

clue.text: Noteworthy character crucial to play missing first of cues

parts.note: an actor's part is the character played

indicators.note: to play suggests the letters can be moved around freely
missing says a letter is left out of crucial
first of picks out only the opening letter of the word cues, the one that goes missing

explanation.surface: An actor's key role in a play goes wrong when the first cue is missed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'missing first of cues' takes the C out of CRUCIAL, and 'to play' rearranges RUCIAL into ICULAR.
explanation.definitionFit: Particular can mean special or worth noting, a synonym for noteworthy.

clue.text: Ruth nurses Earl, showing devotion

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so the earl goes inside

parts.note: ruth is an old word for pity or compassion

explanation.surface: A woman called Ruth nurses an earl back to health, showing her loyalty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ruth' looks like a woman's name, but it is the old word for compassion.
explanation.definitionFit: Piety is religious devotion and reverence, so it is a synonym.

clue.text: This country's announced an edict

indicators.note: announced says the letters are said out loud as you-kays

parts.note: in a British paper this country is the UK, so this is UK's

explanation.surface: The British government has issued a decree.
explanation.walkthrough: Spoken quickly, UK's sounds like the Russian word.
explanation.definitionFit: A ukase was a decree issued by the Russian tsar, so it is an order or decree.

clue.text: Shut up about Penny performing with love rival

parts.note: O is love, the zero score in tennis

indicators.note: the confined word goes round the penny and performing letters

parts.note: pent, as in pent up, means shut up or confined
a show is on when it is being performed

explanation.surface: Someone is locked up after a penny-pinching show with a rival in love.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' means the confined word goes round both the penny and performing letters; the love letter goes at the front. 'love rival' reads as one phrase, but only 'rival' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An opponent is someone who competes against you, a synonym for rival.

clue.text: Pass by a porky footballer

parts.note: to go by is to pass, so go means pass
a porky, short for porky pie, is Cockney rhyming slang for a lie

explanation.surface: A fat footballer is walked past by the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'porky' looks like 'fat', but it is Cockney rhyming slang: porky pie rhymes with lie.
explanation.definitionFit: A goalie is a goalkeeper, an example of a footballer.

clue.text: In extremes of necessity male resorted to wit

indicators.note: In says the jumbled word goes between the outer letters
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters, here of necessity
resorted means sorted again, so the letters of male are rearranged

explanation.surface: When really needed, a man fell back on his humour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'resorted' looks like 'turned to', but it means sorted again, an anagram of male; 'In' puts that inside the outer letters of necessity.
explanation.definitionFit: Namely and to wit are both phrases that introduce a specific example, so they are synonyms.

clue.text: Edward's back in race, dead set

indicators.note: in places the reversed name inside the racing word

parts.note: to hare is to run very fast, to race

indicators.note: back means the name is read backwards

parts.note: Ned is a short form of Edward

explanation.surface: Edward returns to a race he is determined to win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' reverses Edward's short name, and 'in' puts it inside the racing word. 'dead set' reads as one phrase, but only 'set' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Something hardened has become firm, just as concrete is set.
